title: Stable coresets: Unleashing the power of uniform sampling
claim: Cheap uniform sampling matches the approximation error of costlier importance-sampling coresets as coreset size grows, across datasets.
layout: 3 panels in a row, each a line plot with shaded bands
description: Three side-by-side line plots, titled (a) YT, (b) Twitter and (c) SCGE. Each plot has coreset size on the x-axis, from about 150 to 1000. The y-axis is relative error in percent. Each plot shows three curves. Uniform sampling is a solid blue line. Strong coreset with 2 iterations is an orange dashed line. Strong coreset with 1 iteration is a green dashed line. Pale shaded bands of matching colors show one standard deviation. The legend sits in the top right of each panel. In YT and Twitter the curves are noisy and the bands are wide at small sizes, then the curves flatten near zero. In SCGE the error falls smoothly and the three curves converge. The eye goes first to the overlapping blue, orange and green curves and the large bands on the left.
caption: Tradeoff between coreset size and relative error, comparing importance sampling-based coresets with uniform sampling-based coresets across three datasets. Shaded regions represent one standard deviation.
abstract: Uniform sampling is a highly efficient method for data summarization. However, its effectiveness in producing coresets for clustering problems is not yet well understood, primarily because it generally does not yield a strong coreset, which is the prevailing notion in the literature. We formulate \emph{stable coresets}, a notion that is intermediate between the standard notions of weak and strong coresets, and effectively combines the broad applicability of strong coresets with highly efficient constructions, through uniform sampling, of weak coresets. Our main result is that a uniform sample of size $O(Îµ^{-2}\log d)$ yields, with high constant probability, a stable coreset for $1$-median in $\mathbb{R}^d$ under the $\ell_1$ metric. We then leverage the powerful properties of stable coresets to easily derive new coreset constructions, all through uniform sampling, for $\ell_1$ and related metrics, such as Kendall-tau and Jaccard. We also show applications to fair rank aggregation and to approximation algorithms for $k$-median problem in these metric spaces. Our experiments validate the benefits of stable coresets in practice, in terms of both construction time and approximation quality.
